caseVolume.title: Case volume growth
caseVolume.content:
Case volume growth is the year-over-year change in the number of cases Sysco ships -- a volume measure, independent of price/inflation and mix.

For Sysco Corporation: management guides and is judged on local (independent-restaurant) case growth specifically, since local accounts carry higher gross margins than multi-unit/national chain accounts; total case growth can mask a mix shift between the two.

What to watch:

  • Case growth turning negative (as it did in Q3 FY2025) versus revenue still rising on inflation/price
  • Local case growth outpacing total case growth (favorable mix)

segmentOperatingIncome.title: Operating income by segment
segmentOperatingIncome.content:
Sysco runs three reportable operating segments -- U.S. Foodservice Operations (Broadline plus the specialty platforms: FreshPoint, Buckhead/Newport Meat, Greco & Sons, Edward Don), International Foodservice Operations and SYGMA/Other -- plus an unallocated Corporate cost center.

For Sysco Corporation: U.S. Foodservice supplies nearly all of segment operating income; International has been the fastest-growing profit contributor; Corporate is a permanent drag, not a segment to expect positive.

What to watch:

  • International operating margin closing the gap with the U.S. segment
  • Corporate costs growing faster than consolidated revenue

segmentRevenue.title: Revenue by segment
segmentRevenue.content:
Segment revenue split between U.S. Foodservice Operations (~70% of sales), International Foodservice Operations (Canada, UK, France, Ireland, Sweden, and Latin America/Caribbean) and Other (SYGMA's chain-restaurant distribution plus hotel supply).

For Sysco Corporation: International is the segment management is actively growing, both organically and via local case volume; SYGMA/Other is a lower-margin, largely flat-to-declining contractual channel.

What to watch:

  • International revenue growing faster than the U.S. segment
  • SYGMA/Other share of total revenue shrinking as the specialty platforms take share instead

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Sysco Corporation: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Sysco Corporation: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Sysco Corporation: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Sysco Corporation: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Sysco Corporation: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Sysco Corporation: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Sysco Corporation: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Sysco Corporation: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Sysco Corporation: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Sysco Corporation: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
